title: Love, and do what you will
hookLine: Augustine's sermon line: if love is the root, only good can grow

cards: It shows up on posters, in wedding speeches, sometimes tattooed on a forearm. Love, and do what you will. On its own, it can sound like permission for anything: feel it, then follow it.
But the line wasn't written for a poster. Augustine said it in a sermon on the First Letter of John, to a church in North Africa. In context it's close to the opposite of anything goes.
Augustine makes it a test, and a harder one than any rulebook.

teach.b: First, the letter he's preaching on. First John says it plainly. In the Douay-Rheims: "He that loveth not, knoweth not God: for God is charity."
If God is love, Augustine reasons, then love isn't one virtue among many. It's the root. Second, his example.
A father corrects his son sternly. A kidnapper speaks to the boy sweetly. Judge by the outside, and the kidnapper looks kinder.
Judge by the root, and the father is the one who loves. The same action, he says, can come from love or from its opposite.
Third, the line itself, in Latin: dilige, et quod vis fac. Love, and do what you will. Then he spells it out.
If you keep quiet, keep quiet from love. If you cry out, cry out from love. If you correct someone, correct from love.
If you spare someone, spare from love. Let the root of love be within, he says, and from that root nothing but good can grow. Fourth, why this is harder.
A rule asks: did you do the right thing? Augustine asks: why did you do it? You can follow every rule and still act from pride, or spite, or fear.
And you can't fake a root.
So love, and do what you will isn't a loophole.
It's an inspection, down below the soil, where only you and God can see.

how: Catholic preachers and teachers who quote Augustine's line from his homilies on First John tend to set it back in its sermon, where he spells it out as a test of motives: keep quiet, cry out, correct or spare, but from love.

games.q: a father corrects his son sternly. a stranger who means harm speaks to the boy sweetly. Augustine asks: which one acts from love?
games.why: the father. judged from the outside, the stranger looks kinder. judged by the root, love is with the father.

practice: Think of one thing you'll do anyway today, a reply to a message, making dinner, telling someone no, and ask Augustine's question: what's the root?

If it's irritation, or wanting to look good, look for a second root underneath, real care for the person or the task, and rest there for a few breaths. If you pray, ask God for that love before you begin.

wordCard.voice: Love. For Augustine, the root everything else grows from: love, and do what you will. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: love, then do. Whatever you do today, the root decides what grows. Until tomorrow.
